newsitem.title: MOZAMBIQUE: Maputo Corridor boosted by smelter, ministers say.
newsitem.headline: Maputo Corridor boosted by smelter, ministers say.

text.p: A development corridor to link South Africa's industrial heart and its nearest port Maputo, Mozambique's capital, has been boosted by the go-ahead for a huge aluminium smelter, the two governments said on Friday.
Ministers from both southern African states told a conference on the "Maputo Corridor" that work on upgrading road and rail links and port facilities should begin in 1998.
"The infrastructure projects must be delivered on time," South African Transport Minister Mac Maharaj warned at the meeting but he said work was on schedule so far.
"Our record to date dispels any pessimism," he added.
The corridor, from the Johannesburg area to the coast 500 km (300 miles) away, was launched in May 1996 by presidents Nelson Mandela and Joaquim Chissano.

The aim is to upgrade road and rail links to promote the development of mining, agriculture, manufacturing and tourism along the route and to dredge and improve Maputo harbour. South Africa's main port, Durban, is further from Johannesburg and is already overstretched.

In the early 1970s 40 percent of South African-manufactured goods for export passed through Maputo. Independence in 1975 from Portgual sparked a 16-year civil war and Mozambique, for years the world's poorest country, became a no-go zone.

Trevor Jackson, chief executive of the Franco-South African TRAC consortium which was awarded the contract for the $400 million toll road in May, said construction should begin in record time, by February, for completion in 2001.

Mozambique's Transport Minister, Paul Muxanga, said the contract for upgrading Maputo harbour should be awarded the same month, after a preferred bidder is announced on December 18 So work should begin by mid-year.

The port, road, rail and related infrastructure projects -- including a faster new border crossing, telecommunications and electrification -- will cost in excess of $1 billion and 90 percent of this is to be private-sector investment.
Officials said related private investments of some $3.5 billion, mostly for the aluminium smelter, an iron reduction plant and other heavy industries, were under consideration.
The jewel in the crown to date is the $1.1 billion Mozal smelter outside Maputo, to be operated by Alusaf Ltd, which the company's parent Gencor Ltd GCOR.O approved in June.

"This mega-project is almost 100 percent approved, with only a few fundamentals in the feasibility of the project to be finalised, and construction is scheduled for October," said Maharaj. The first metal production is expected in 2000.
Muxanga said electrification projects had been brought forward to service the investment initiatives such as Mozal.

One $105 million project will bring power from a station run by South Africa's Eskom in the east of the country to Maputo. Another, costing twice as much, will harness hydro-electric power on the Zambezi river in Mozambique.

"It is only through building efficient and effective road, rail and port links with backup of power and telecommunications that we can unlock the potential in this region," Maharaj said. "It is a potential that cannot be underestimated."
